questions.q: Which statement best matches the chapter's meaning of a 'maritime neighbour'?
questions.a: The box in the chapter defines it as a country connected by a shared sea or ocean, even without a land border. The other options turn it into trade, coastline or port use.
o: A country linked to another by a shared sea or ocean, with no direct land border needed
A country whose ships carry goods to India's ports across the Indian Ocean every year
A country with a long coastline that also shares a land boundary with India
A country that uses India's ports as gateways for its own imports and exports

questions.q: A relief ship leaves Kochi for a flooded island country, and at the same time the Mundra port clears cargo for several nations. Which idea in the chapter do both events illustrate?
questions.a: The chapter says India's ports are gateways for trade and her central position helps in timely aid; such involvement is called regionalism. The other terms name kinds of neighbourhood or land.
o: Regionalism, working together for the benefit of the region
The traditional view of neighbourhood based on land borders
The Indian Ocean being the largest ocean in the world
An archipelago, a group of islands lying close together

questions.q:
Match the figure in Column A with what it measures in Column B.
Column A: 1. Total land boundary  2. Coastline  3. Share of the world's container ships in the Indian Ocean  4. People in the countries the ocean connects
Column B: a. About 11,100 km  b. About 15,100 km  c. One-half  d. About 2.7 billion
questions.a: Land boundary is about 15,100 km, coastline about 11,100 km, container ships one-half, and about 2.7 billion people live in the countries the ocean connects. The distractors swap the two lengths or the share with the people count.

questions.q:
Read the statements about India's neighbourhood.
1. India's land boundary runs through deserts, plains, forests, mountains, marshes and river valleys.
2. Only a country that shares a land boundary with India is treated as a neighbour in this chapter.
3. The Indian Ocean connects many countries that are home to around 2.7 billion people.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are stated in the chapter. 2 is false because the chapter also treats Sri Lanka, the Maldives and others across the sea as neighbours.

questions.q: In the traditional view of neighbourhood described in the chapter, which of these is NOT counted as a neighbour of India?
questions.a: The traditional view counts only countries sharing a land boundary. Sri Lanka lies across the water, so it comes in only through the wider view; Bhutan, Myanmar and Bangladesh share land boundaries.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India's central position in the Indian Ocean helps her give timely humanitarian aid and disaster relief in the region.
Reason (R): The Indian Ocean is the third-largest ocean in the world.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but the size ranking of the ocean does not explain why India's central position helps her send quick aid. The explanation is her position and her ports.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Meenal looks at a list of India's neighbours and says, 'Oman cannot be a neighbour, because India and Oman do not touch.' Which idea from the chapter shows her mistake?
questions.a: A maritime neighbour needs no land border; Oman and India are linked by a shared sea. Oman has no land boundary with India, is not in the SAARC list, and the 32 km figure is the Palk Strait gap to Sri Lanka, not a rule.
o: A shared sea or ocean can make countries neighbours with no land border
Oman shares a stretch of the land boundary through the state of Gujarat
Oman is a SAARC member, so it counts in the neighbourhood
Maritime neighbours must lie within about 32 km of India

questions.q: The chapter says the Indian Ocean carries about what share of the world's oil?
questions.a: Two-thirds of the world's oil moves through the Indian Ocean. Half is the figure for container ships and one-third is the figure for bulk cargo.

questions.q: Explain how the shape and position of India's peninsula make her 'a vital link' in the region, and what she is able to do because of it.
questions.a: Her peninsula extends deep into the Indian Ocean, giving access to important sea routes and linking Southeast Asia, West Asia and Africa. This lets her play a key role in trade and regional cooperation and provide timely humanitarian aid and disaster relief.
s: Peninsula extends into the Indian Ocean, with access to sea routes
Links Southeast Asia, West Asia and Africa
Role in trade, regional cooperation and quick aid

questions.q: The chapter calls India 'a maritime nation'. Give two facts from the chapter that support this description.
questions.a: India is surrounded by sea on three sides, and has a coastline of about 11,100 km; her peninsula extends deep into the Indian Ocean. Any two.
s: First supporting fact such as the sea on three sides
Second supporting fact such as the 11,100 km coastline or peninsula extending into the ocean

questions.q:
A club studying the Indian Ocean imagines one month in which the world's sea shipments are 3,600 oil cargoes, 2,400 bulk cargoes and 1,800 container cargoes. It wants to know how many of each would move through the Indian Ocean, using the shares given in the chapter.
(a) How many of the oil cargoes would move through the Indian Ocean?
(b) Give the bulk-cargo figure and the container figure separately.
(c) Which feature of India's position, according to the chapter, makes her a vital link for this traffic?
(d) The club has space to feature only one cargo type on its poster, to show how important the ocean is. Which should it choose? Compare the shares and the numbers.
questions.a: (a) 3,600 x 2/3 = 2,400. (b) Bulk 2,400 x 1/3 = 800; container 1,800 x 1/2 = 900. (c) Her peninsula extends deep into the Indian Ocean, linking Southeast Asia, West Asia and Africa. (d) Oil: it has the biggest share (two-thirds, against one-half for containers and one-third for bulk) and the largest number of cargoes (2,400 against 900 and 800).
s: Part (a): 2,400 oil cargoes
Part (b): 800 bulk and 900 container
Part (c): peninsula extends into the ocean, linking Southeast Asia, West Asia and Africa
Part (d): oil, backed by both the largest share and the largest number

questions.q: Differentiate between the traditional view of neighbourhood and the wider view used in this chapter.
questions.a: The traditional view counts countries sharing a land boundary. The wider view also includes maritime neighbours linked by sea, such as Sri Lanka, the Maldives, Oman and Singapore.
s: Traditional view: neighbours are countries sharing a land boundary
Wider view: includes maritime neighbours linked by sea, with an example

questions.q: What is regionalism? Give one way, from the chapter, in which India shows it.
questions.a: Regionalism is working together for the benefit of everyone in the region, creating peace, stability and shared progress. Example: India's ports as gateways or humanitarian aid and disaster relief.
s: Defines regionalism as working together for the benefit of the region
Gives one correct example such as disaster relief or port gateways

questions.q: Karan says, 'India's land boundary of about 15,100 km is shared with all her neighbours, so Sri Lanka and the Maldives are covered in that figure.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. The 15,100 km figure is for the land boundary, which is shared only with land neighbours such as Pakistan, Nepal and Myanmar. Sri Lanka and the Maldives are across the water and are linked by the sea, not by a land boundary.
s: Verdict: disagrees with Karan
Reason: the 15,100 km is a land boundary and Sri Lanka and the Maldives lie across the sea
Names two actual land neighbours such as Pakistan and Nepal

questions.q: (a) Which two countries does the chapter place in the northwest of India's land neighbourhood? (b) Sri Lanka is called an immediate neighbour but is missing from that land list. Why?
questions.a: (a) Pakistan and Afghanistan. (b) Sri Lanka lies across the water, so it is a neighbour through the sea and not through a land boundary.
s: Part (a): Pakistan and Afghanistan
Part (b): Sri Lanka is a neighbour across the water, with no land boundary

questions.q: Compare the 'traditional' neighbourhood with the 'maritime' neighbourhood of India on who is included and what links them to India. Then state one benefit of the maritime link, and analyse why the chapter chooses the wider view.
questions.a: Traditional: Pakistan, Afghanistan, China's Tibet, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar; linked by a land boundary of about 15,100 km through varied landscapes. Maritime: Sri Lanka and the Maldives (immediate) and Iran, Oman, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia; linked by a shared sea or ocean. Benefit of the sea link: centuries of trade and cultural exchange. The chapter uses the wider view to place India's central and strategic position in South Asia.
s: Traditional neighbours named and linked by a land boundary of about 15,100 km
Maritime neighbours named, immediate and wider
Link by sea: a shared sea or ocean, in contrast to land
One benefit of the maritime link such as trade or cultural exchange
Reason for the wider view: India's central and strategic place

questions.q:
The social science club of a Visakhapatnam school is making a notice board called 'Our Neighbours'. Seven cards are ready: Bhutan, Maldives, Bangladesh, Thailand, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Singapore. Tara wants a board only for countries that share India's land boundary. Rohan wants all seven cards on the board under two headings, so that it shows the view of neighbourhood taken in the chapter.
(a) Sort the seven cards under 'land neighbour' and 'maritime neighbour'.
(b) Using the chapter's figures, by how many km is India's land boundary longer than her coastline?
(c) Which idea in the chapter shows that a board with only land neighbours leaves something out?
(d) The club's aim is to show how the chapter defines India's neighbourhood. Whose board serves this aim better? Support your answer with a count of the cards and a chapter fact.
questions.a: (a) Land: Bhutan, Bangladesh, Nepal. Maritime: Maldives, Thailand, Sri Lanka, Singapore. (b) 15,100 - 11,100 = 4,000 km. (c) Neighbours are not only those sharing a land border; a maritime neighbour is joined by a shared sea or ocean. (d) Rohan's board: Tara's board would carry only 3 of the 7 cards and drop 4 maritime neighbours, while the chapter uses the wider view that includes countries across the sea.
s: Part (a): correct sorting into land and maritime
Part (b): 4,000 km, from the two chapter figures
Part (c): maritime neighbours need no land border; neighbourhood is not only about borders
Part (d): Rohan's board, using the 3-of-7 count and the wider view

questions.q: (a) Write the share of bulk cargo and the share of oil that the chapter gives for the Indian Ocean. (b) Which of the two is the bigger share, and what does that suggest about the ocean to a shipping company?
questions.a: (a) Bulk cargo one-third, oil two-thirds. (b) Oil is the bigger share; it suggests the Indian Ocean is a very busy route that world trade depends on.
s: Part (a): one-third of bulk cargo and two-thirds of oil
Part (b): oil is bigger, showing a busy route important to world shipping

questions.q: 'Being good neighbours is not just about borders, but also about working together for the benefit of everyone in the region.' Justify this statement using the Indian Ocean and India's role in the region.
questions.a: Border is only one side: Sri Lanka, the Maldives and others are neighbours across the sea. The Indian Ocean carries half the world's container ships, one-third of bulk cargo and two-thirds of oil and connects countries with 2.7 billion people. India's ports serve as gateways and her position helps in aid and disaster relief. Such involvement is regionalism, creating peace, stability and shared progress.
s: Explains that neighbours exist beyond land borders, with maritime examples
Uses at least two Indian Ocean facts
Mentions India's ports and central position and aid
Names regionalism and its aims: peace, stability, shared progress
Draws a clear concluding judgement linking borders and cooperation

questions.q: Prepare a three-line notice for a Class 6 display board titled 'Neighbours without a border'. Each line must use a different fact from the chapter.
questions.a: Any three correct lines, e.g. Sri Lanka lies across the Palk Strait by sea; the Maldives and others are immediate maritime neighbours; Iran, Oman, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia are part of the wider maritime neighbourhood.
s: Line 1 is a correct fact on maritime neighbours
Line 2 is correct and different from line 1
Line 3 is correct and the notice makes the point that neighbours need not share land

questions.q: Which of the following does NOT lie along the border between India and China, as listed in the chapter?
questions.a: The border runs across Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Ladakh. Mizoram touches Myanmar, not China.

questions.q: Which pair of monks travelled from China to Indian centres of learning, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Faxian and Xuanzang came from China to India. Bodhidharma, Dharmakshema and Kumarajiva went from India to China; Mahendra and Sanghamitra went to Sri Lanka.

questions.q: The chapter says the balance of trade between India and China is 'much in China's favour'. What does this mean?
questions.a: China's exports to India are worth about eight times India's exports to China. It does not refer to area, to company numbers or to who sells more.
o: China sells India goods worth about eight times what India sells to China
India sells China goods worth about eight times what she buys from China
China is about eight times larger than India in area
Chinese companies run eight times as many offices in India as the reverse

questions.q:
Read the statements about India and China.
1. Only Indian monks, and never Chinese monks, travelled along the routes linking the two countries.
2. In the 13th century Hindu merchants built temples in the Chinese port city of Quanzhou.
3. China is approximately three times larger than India in area.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 are stated in the chapter. 1 is false: Faxian and Xuanzang, Chinese monks, travelled to India.

questions.q: The chapter says India and China have shared a long and strategic relationship since which year?
questions.a: The chapter dates this relationship from 1950. 1947 is the year of Partition and 1971 the year Bangladesh was born; 1985 is when SAARC was formed.

questions.q: Compare the cultural link and the trade link between India and China. Which has been more balanced, and why? Use at least two facts for each.
questions.a: Cultural link: Buddhism from India reached China in the 1st century CE; Indian monks went to China and Chinese monks to India; Hindu merchants built temples in Quanzhou. It has moved in both directions. Trade link: India exports iron ore, chemicals and cotton yarn and imports electronics and industrial equipment, but China's exports are about eight times India's. So the cultural exchange has been more balanced, while trade is heavily in China's favour.
s: Two facts on the cultural link
Two facts on the trade link
Concludes culture is more balanced and trade is one-sided, with the reason

questions.q: Where is the Kaiyuan temple, who built it, and what do its pillars show?
questions.a: It is in the port city of Quanzhou, China. Hindu merchants built temples there in the 13th century, and the pillars show Vishnu, Shiva and stories from the Ramayana and the Puranas.
s: Location: Quanzhou, a Chinese port and trading centre
Builders and carvings: Hindu merchants; Vishnu, Shiva, Ramayana and Puranas stories

questions.q: Ravi says, 'Even though China sells far more to India than India sells to China, trade between the two continues, and companies of each country have set up operations in the other.' Do you agree? Support your answer with the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says the balance of trade is much in China's favour, since her exports are worth about eight times India's. It also says trade continues, with India selling iron ore, chemicals and cotton yarn, and that several Indian companies operate in China and vice versa. Ravi's claim is supported on both counts.
s: Verdict: agrees with Ravi
Supports the first half with the imbalance of about eight times
Supports the second half with continuing trade or companies in each country

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Kaiyuan temple in Quanzhou has pillars carved with Vishnu, Shiva and stories from the Ramayana.
Reason (R): Quanzhou was an important trading centre where Hindu merchants built temples in the 13th century.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, and the presence of Hindu merchants who built temples there explains why such carvings are found.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A cotton-yarn firm in Tiruppur sells to a Chinese buyer, while a Delhi shop stocks Chinese-made mobile phones. What do the two facts together show about the trade between the two countries?
questions.a: Goods move both ways, so trade is real, but China sells far more to India. The other options claim no Indian exports, a stopped trade or an even balance, which the chapter denies.
o: Goods move both ways, though China sells far more
India only buys from China and sells nothing in return
Trade has stopped because of the border tensions
The value of goods moving each way is nearly equal

questions.q: On a school trip to a Chinese port, Aditi sees stone pillars carved with Vishnu rescuing an elephant from a crocodile. What best explains the carvings?
questions.a: In the 13th century Hindu merchants built temples in Quanzhou, a trading port, and the Kaiyuan temple has such carvings. Monks of the 1st century and Chinese pilgrims are linked to Buddhism, not these temples.
o: Hindu merchants built temples at the trading port of Quanzhou in the 13th century
Indian monks carried these stories with Buddhism to China in the 1st century CE
Chinese monks like Xuanzang copied the carvings from Indian centres of learning
The carvings were placed there to mark the India-China border in the Himalayas

questions.q:
At a Pune school debate, the teacher says that the gap between China's exports to India and India's exports to China in a certain year was Rs 7 lakh crore. The students must use the chapter's ratio of the two trade flows.
(a) What were India's exports to China that year?
(b) What were China's exports to India?
(c) Name two goods that India sells to China, as given in the chapter.
(d) Team A proposes that India double her exports to China. Team B proposes that India buy one-quarter less from China. Find the new gap under each plan, say which narrows the gap more, and name one chapter fact that makes that plan hard to carry out.
questions.a: (a) The gap is 8x - x = 7x = 7, so India's exports were Rs 1 lakh crore. (b) 8 x 1 = Rs 8 lakh crore. (c) Any two of iron ore, chemicals, cotton yarn. (d) Team A: 8 - 2 = Rs 6 lakh crore. Team B: 8 x 3/4 = 6, and 6 - 1 = Rs 5 lakh crore. Team B narrows the gap more. It is hard because the imports are electronics such as mobile phones and computer hardware and industrial equipment, which have to be bought from somewhere else.
s: Part (a): Rs 1 lakh crore, using the ratio of about eight times
Part (b): Rs 8 lakh crore
Part (c): two correct goods exported to China
Part (d): gaps of Rs 6 and Rs 5 lakh crore, Team B better, with a chapter fact on the imported goods

questions.q: State two links between India and China from the chapter that are not about trade.
questions.a: Any two: Buddhism reached China around the 1st century CE; monks travelled in both directions; Hindu merchants built temples such as the Kaiyuan temple at Quanzhou.
s: First non-trade link, correctly stated
Second non-trade link, different from the first

questions.q: (a) Name one Indian monk who carried Buddhism to China and one Chinese monk who travelled to India. (b) What did these journeys create between the two countries?
questions.a: (a) Indian: Bodhidharma, Dharmakshema or Kumarajiva; Chinese: Faxian or Xuanzang. (b) Deep spiritual and intellectual ties.
s: Part (a): one correct Indian monk and one correct Chinese monk
Part (b): spiritual and intellectual ties

questions.q: Explain how Buddhism became a bridge between India and China. Mention where it began, when it reached China, how it travelled and who took it there.
questions.a: Buddhism began in India and reached China around the 1st century CE through trade and pilgrimage routes. Indian monks like Bodhidharma, Dharmakshema and Kumarajiva carried its teachings, while Chinese monks like Faxian and Xuanzang visited Indian centres of learning.
s: Originated in India and reached China around the 1st century CE
Routes of trade and pilgrimage
Names monks going in each direction

questions.q:
A Kolkata school builds an exhibition called 'Silk and Sacred Paths' with three panels. Panel 1 shows a monk leaving India with scrolls; Panel 2 shows a harbour scene with carved pillars; Panel 3 is a 2024-25 table in which India sells iron ore, chemicals and cotton yarn and buys phones, computer hardware and industrial equipment. The school's aim is to show visitors that the relationship has run in both directions. Space allows one more panel.
(a) Name the Chinese port and the temple Panel 2 should show.
(b) Name one Indian monk suited to Panel 1 and the century in which Buddhism reached China.
(c) Which panel shows an exchange that is one-sided, and what figure from the chapter proves it?
(d) The extra panel can be either 'monks travelling in both directions' or 'the trade imbalance'. Which better serves the school's aim, given what the three panels already show? Justify it.
questions.a: (a) Quanzhou and the Kaiyuan temple. (b) Bodhidharma, Dharmakshema or Kumarajiva; around the 1st century CE. (c) Panel 3, the trade table; China's exports to India are about eight times India's exports to China. (d) Monks in both directions: the imbalance is already shown by Panel 3, and Panel 1 shows only an Indian monk leaving, whereas the chapter says Chinese monks like Faxian and Xuanzang also travelled to India, which shows a two-way link.
s: Part (a): Quanzhou and the Kaiyuan temple
Part (b): correct monk and the 1st century CE
Part (c): Panel 3 and the eight-times figure
Part (d): monks in both directions, with the reason that Panel 3 already shows the imbalance and Panel 1 shows one direction only

questions.q: What is the main cause of the tensions between India and China mentioned in the chapter, and name two ways in which efforts are being made to resolve them.
questions.a: The tensions are mostly related to the shared borders. Efforts include trade, dialogue and border resolution mechanisms.
s: Tensions mostly related to shared borders
Two ways: any two of trade, dialogue, border resolution mechanisms

questions.q: Suppose India's exports to China in a year are worth Rs 1.2 lakh crore. (a) Using the chapter's ratio, what would China's exports to India be worth? (b) By how much would China's exports exceed India's, and what does that gap say about the balance of trade?
questions.a: (a) 1.2 x 8 = Rs 9.6 lakh crore. (b) 9.6 - 1.2 = Rs 8.4 lakh crore more; the balance is heavily in China's favour.
s: Part (a): Rs 9.6 lakh crore
Part (b): gap of Rs 8.4 lakh crore, balance much in China's favour

questions.q: 'India and China share a relationship of both cooperation and tension.' Justify this statement with evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: Cooperation: Buddhism and monks, temples at Quanzhou, continuing trade (iron ore, chemicals, cotton yarn out; electronics and industrial equipment in), companies in each other's country. Tension: heightened tensions in recent years mostly over shared borders and a few serious conflicts, with an imbalance in trade of about eight times in China's favour. Efforts at trade, dialogue and border resolution mechanisms show both sides try to manage it.
s: Cooperation evidence from culture
Cooperation evidence from trade and companies
Tension evidence from the borders and conflicts
Notes the trade imbalance of about eight times
Mentions efforts at dialogue and a balanced conclusion

questions.q: Show that the statement 'Buddhism came from China to India around the 1st century CE' cannot be right, using two facts from the chapter.
questions.a: The chapter says Buddhism originated in India and reached China around the 1st century CE through trade and pilgrimage routes, carried by Indian monks such as Bodhidharma and Kumarajiva. So it travelled from India to China, not the other way; Chinese monks like Faxian and Xuanzang came later to study at Indian centres.
s: States that Buddhism originated in India
States that it reached China around the 1st century CE by trade and pilgrimage routes
Names Indian monks who carried it, or concludes that the direction was India to China

questions.q:
Match the place in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Kartarpur Corridor  2. Katas Raj  3. Hinglaj Mata Mandir  4. Dera Baba Nanak
Column B: a. An ancient shrine in Balochistan  b. A temple complex with a sacred pond  c. The crossing opened in 2019 for pilgrims going to Kartarpur  d. Where binoculars once let devotees view Kartarpur
questions.a: Kartarpur Corridor is the crossing opened in 2019; Katas Raj has a sacred pond; Hinglaj Mata Mandir is in Balochistan; Dera Baba Nanak is where binoculars were set up. The distractors swap the two places in Pakistan or the corridor and the viewing point.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. India's land border with Bangladesh is shorter than her border with China.
2. Before the 1947 Partition, Pakistan was a part of India.
3. Bangladesh, earlier called East Pakistan, was born in 1971 as the outcome of a war between India and Pakistan.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 are stated in the chapter. 1 is false: the chapter says the land border with Bangladesh is even longer than the border with China.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The India-Pakistan border stretches across Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab and the union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
Reason (R): The Katas Raj temple complex, linked to the Mahabharata, lies in Pakistan's Punjab.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but the location of a temple does not explain which Indian states the border passes through.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT named in the chapter as something that continues to bridge the India-Pakistan border?
questions.a: The chapter lists languages, cuisines, music and festivals as bridges. A common currency is not mentioned.

questions.q: Where does the larger part of the Sundarbans, the largest mangrove forest in the world, lie?
questions.a: About two-thirds of the forest lies in Bangladesh and the rest in India. The other options reverse the share or split it equally.

questions.q: The Kartarpur Corridor was officially opened in 2019 to mark which occasion?
questions.a: The corridor opened to mark Guru Nanak's 550th birth anniversary. The other options use dates or events from the same section but not the reason for the opening.
o: The end of the Kargil War in 1999

questions.q: After a severe cyclone, villages sheltered behind a mangrove forest on the India-Bangladesh coast suffer less damage than villages far from it. Which feature of the Sundarbans does this show?
questions.a: The chapter says the forest serves as a barrier to cyclones. Being a home for the Bengal tiger and a World Heritage Site are true but do not explain lower damage.
o: It serves as a barrier to cyclones
It is home to the Bengal tiger
It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site
It lies mostly within India's borders

questions.q: Gurpreet's grandmother lives in Dera Baba Nanak in Punjab and wishes to visit the Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Kartarpur. What does the chapter say about how she can go today?
questions.a: She can use the Kartarpur Corridor, which needs a permit and no visa. The passport-only rule belongs to the India-Nepal open border, and the binocular viewing was the situation before 2019.
o: She can go through the corridor with a permit and no visa
She needs only her passport, as under the open border with Nepal
She must get both a visa and a permit for the corridor
She can only view the gurdwara from a distance, through binoculars

questions.q: Name the wars between India and Pakistan mentioned in the chapter, with their years, and the full-scale conflict of 1999.
questions.a: Wars in 1948, 1965 and 1971; the Kargil War in 1999.
s: Wars in 1948, 1965 and 1971
Kargil War, 1999

questions.q: Simran says, 'Even with the wars and the terrorist attacks, there have been periods of trade and pilgrimage routes opened between India and Pakistan.' Do you agree? Support your answer from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says the tumultuous journey has also been marked by attempts at peace, such as periods of trade and the opening of pilgrimage routes for Hindu and Sikh pilgrims, and it names shrines such as Katas Raj and Hinglaj Mata Mandir. It adds that the attacks have still prevented normal relations, so the claim is true but does not say that peace has been reached.
s: Verdict: agrees with Simran
Names periods of trade or opened pilgrimage routes
Gives a shared shrine and notes that normal relations are still prevented

questions.q: (a) Name the five Indian states along the land border with Bangladesh. (b) Rohan says it touches Sikkim too. Is he right? Give the chapter's evidence.
questions.a: (a) West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. (b) No. Sikkim is listed among the states on the borders with China, Nepal and Bhutan, not with Bangladesh.
s: Part (a): all five states named
Part (b): Sikkim is not on the list, it borders China, Nepal and Bhutan

questions.q:
A joint committee of India and Bangladesh studies the Sundarbans. Suppose the forest covers 9,900 square km and a fund of Rs 30 crore has been set aside for guarding it, a cost that grows with the area guarded. One member wants to divide the fund in proportion to the area in each country; another wants equal shares.
(a) How many square km lie in Bangladesh?
(b) How many square km lie in India?
(c) Why must the two countries coordinate the forest's protection?
(d) Which way of dividing the fund is better supported? Find each country's share under both plans and give your reason.
questions.a: (a) 9,900 x 2/3 = 6,600 sq km. (b) 9,900 - 6,600 = 3,300 sq km. (c) The forest is one ecosystem across two countries, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, a home to the Bengal tiger and a barrier to cyclones. (d) The proportional plan: Bangladesh Rs 20 crore and India Rs 10 crore, matching the two-thirds and one-third of the area. Equal shares of Rs 15 crore each would give too little to guard the larger part and too much for the smaller.
s: Part (a): 6,600 sq km
Part (b): 3,300 sq km
Part (c): one shared forest, coordinated protection, shield from cyclones
Part (d): proportional plan, Rs 20 crore and Rs 10 crore against Rs 15 crore each, tied to area

questions.q: Write three quiz clues, each using a fact from the chapter, for which the answer is 'the Sundarbans'.
questions.a: Any three correct clues: largest mangrove forest of the world; two-thirds in Bangladesh and the rest in India; home to the Bengal tiger; UNESCO World Heritage Site; barrier to cyclones.
s: Clue 1 is a correct chapter fact
Clue 2 is correct and different
Clue 3 is correct and the three together point to the Sundarbans

questions.a: Only 1 is correct. 2 is false: India also helped in the 2014 water crisis and during COVID-19. 3 is false: Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia are not on the member list.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Sri Lanka is India's nearest maritime neighbour.
Reason (R): The Palk Strait between India and Sri Lanka is about 320 km wide at its nearest point.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: the Palk Strait is only about 32 km wide at the nearest point.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Which Dhivehi word does the chapter link with the Sanskrit word 'matsya'?
questions.a: Mas, meaning fish, echoes matsya. Raajje echoes raja (king), while dhoni (boat) and kukulhu (chicken) share roots with Tamil and Malayalam.

questions.q: A student's timeline for a display reads: (i) Buddhism reaches Sri Lanka in the 3rd century CE through Mahendra and Sanghamitra; (ii) SAARC is formed in 1985; (iii) the Maldives becomes independent in 1965; (iv) Sri Lanka's civil war runs from the mid-1980s to around 2010. Find the one entry that is wrong, correct it, and show that the other entries match the chapter.
questions.a: Entry (i) is wrong: Buddhism was introduced in the 3rd century BCE, not CE, by Mahendra and Sanghamitra, the son and daughter of Emperor Ashoka. The other three match the chapter: SAARC was formed in 1985, the Maldives became independent in 1965, and the civil war ran from the mid-1980s to around 2010.
s: Identifies entry (i) as the wrong one
Corrects it to the 3rd century BCE
Shows that the other three entries match the chapter

questions.q: (a) Between whom was Sri Lanka's civil war fought and for roughly how long? (b) Where in India did many Tamil families go?
questions.a: (a) The Sinhalese majority and the Tamil minority, from the mid-1980s to around 2010. (b) South India, especially Tamil Nadu.
s: Part (a): Sinhalese majority versus Tamil minority, mid-1980s to 2010
Part (b): south India, especially Tamil Nadu

questions.q:
In 2009 the president and ministers of an island country held a cabinet meeting under the sea. Suppose the highest point of one of its islands is 1.5 m above sea level. The island council has funds for only one first step and wants to act on the cause of the problem named in the chapter, and not only on its effects.
(a) Which country is this, and by how much could its sea level rise by the end of the century, according to the chapter? How much dry height would the island's highest point have left?
(b) Why did the cabinet meet underwater?
(c) Which Indian-led initiative shares solar technology with this country?
(d) The council can spend first on a sea wall for this island alone, or on joining other nations in solar cooperation and calling world attention to global warming. Which should it choose first? Justify with the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The Maldives; up to 1 metre; 1.5 - 1 = 0.5 m. (b) To draw attention to the danger of rising sea levels owing to global warming. (c) The International Solar Alliance. (d) Joining other nations and calling attention: the chapter ties rising seas to global warming, which no single island can stop, and the Maldives already takes part in the International Solar Alliance; a sea wall treats the effect on one island only.
s: Part (a): the Maldives, up to 1 metre, 0.5 m left
Part (b): to draw attention to rising seas from global warming
Part (c): International Solar Alliance
Part (d): joining others and calling attention, because the cause is global warming

questions.q: 'Regional cooperation like SAARC is valuable even when tensions exist.' Justify this using the chapter.
questions.a: SAARC was formed in 1985 by eight neighbours to promote mutual interests and sociocultural and economic progress, sharing resources in science, education and health. Political tensions have often disrupted it. Yet India's quick help to the Maldives in 2004, 2014 and COVID-19 shows cooperation continues, other regional groups centred on the Indian Ocean exist, and the chapter calls regional involvement a basis for peace, stability and shared progress.
s: SAARC's aim and formation
The areas of sharing: science, education, health
Acknowledges that tensions disrupt it
Gives examples of cooperation continuing, e.g. disaster relief
Reaches a reasoned conclusion

questions.q: (a) What is the width of the Palk Strait at its nearest point, and how far is the Maldives from Minicoy? (b) Which neighbour is nearer to India by these figures, and by how many km?
questions.a: (a) About 32 km; about 130 km. (b) Sri Lanka is nearer, by 130 - 32 = 98 km.
s: Part (a): 32 km and 130 km
Part (b): Sri Lanka, by 98 km

questions.q: Why is the Maldives especially vulnerable to climate change? What did its president and cabinet do in 2009 to draw attention to it?
questions.a: As an island nation, a sea-level rise of up to 1 metre by the end of the century could partly submerge many islands. In 2009 they held a cabinet meeting underwater, 4 m below the surface.
s: Island nation at risk from rising sea level
Underwater cabinet meeting in 2009

questions.q: Explain how a shared challenge can become an opportunity for cooperation, using the Maldives and climate change as your example.
questions.a: The Maldives faces rising sea levels, which could partly submerge islands. It is a member of the International Solar Alliance, an Indian initiative that shares research and technology on solar energy. This joint effort for sustainability shows how a challenge draws partners together.
s: Identifies the challenge of rising sea levels
Mentions the International Solar Alliance as the joint effort
Explains how the link supports long-term cooperation

questions.q: (a) Who introduced Buddhism to Sri Lanka, and in which century? (b) Which other Indian tradition travelled there, and through what?
questions.a: (a) Mahendra and Sanghamitra, son and daughter of Ashoka, in the 3rd century BCE. (b) Hinduism, notably through its two Epics.
s: Part (a): Mahendra and Sanghamitra, 3rd century BCE
Part (b): Hinduism through the two Epics

questions.q:
A Class 7 class in Chennai prepares a display on the island neighbours with six entries: Mahendra and Sanghamitra bring Buddhism to Sri Lanka; the Boduberu dance echoes Tamil rhythms in the Maldives; India helps the Maldives after the 2004 tsunami; India helps in the 2014 water crisis in Male; India helps during COVID-19; Tamil families move to Tamil Nadu during Sri Lanka's civil war. The class wants a heading that fits most of the six entries.
(a) About how many years did Sri Lanka's civil war last, on the chapter's dates?
(b) In which year did the Maldives become independent, and how many years later did the help of 2004 come?
(c) How many of the six entries show India helping or sheltering people in a crisis?
(d) Which heading suits the display better, 'Ancient Bonds' or 'Friends in Need'? Justify with the entries.
questions.a: (a) Mid-1980s to around 2010, about 25 years. (b) 1965; 2004 - 1965 = 39 years. (c) Four: the 2004 tsunami, the 2014 water crisis, COVID-19 and the Tamil families who moved to Tamil Nadu. (d) 'Friends in Need': four of the six entries show help or shelter in a crisis, while only two (Buddhism and the Boduberu dance) belong to ancient and cultural bonds; the chapter also calls India the region's trusted first responder.
s: Part (a): about 25 years
Part (b): 1965 and 39 years
Part (c): four entries
Part (d): 'Friends in Need', backed by the count of four against two

questions.q: The Ayutthaya Kingdom of Thailand, founded in 1351, was named after which Indian city?
questions.a: It was named after Ayodhya, the birthplace of Rama. Dwarka is the city behind the name Dvaravati; Srivijaya is a Malay kingdom and Pataliputra is not linked to a Thai name.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. The Dvaravati culture of Thailand was named after Ayodhya.
2. The Indian community in Malaysia came only in the 15th century, when Islam became predominant.
3. Indonesia is an archipelago with several large islands and over 17,000 smaller ones.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only 3 is correct. 1 is false: Dvaravati refers to Dwarka, Krishna's city. 2 is false: Indian workers migrated to Malaysia in the 19th and 20th centuries.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Tamil is not one of Singapore's official languages.
Reason (R): About 9 per cent of Singapore's residents are of Indian origin, and many of them live in the area called Little India.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false because Tamil is one of Singapore's four official languages, along with English, Mandarin and Malay. R is true: about 9 per cent of residents are of Indian origin and many live in Little India.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: After a strong earthquake under the sea off Sumatra, alerts reach Chennai, Colombo and Bangkok almost together. Which arrangement in the chapter makes this possible?
questions.a: After the 2004 tsunami, India joined Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Thailand and others to set up a network of sensors, satellites and communication links; the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre in Hyderabad alerts neighbours too.
o: A network of sensors and satellites with the Early Warning Centre in Hyderabad
The regional group SAARC and its cultural programmes
The Borobudur Stupa and its mandala design

questions.q: The Borobudur Stupa in Indonesia is built in how many enormous platforms?
questions.a: The chapter says the Borobudur Stupa has a pyramidal shape in five enormous platforms. The other numbers do not appear in this description.

questions.q: Zoya sees a signboard in a Singapore street in four languages: English, Mandarin, Tamil and Malay. What does the presence of Tamil among them suggest, according to the chapter?
questions.a: It suggests long and close contact between south India and Singapore, through traders, monks and Indian-origin residents. Singapore was part of Malaysia only until 1965, Buddhism is the most widely practised religion but not the only one, and about 9 per cent of residents are of Indian origin.
o: Long and close contact between south India and Singapore
That Singapore is still a part of Malaysia
That Buddhism is the only religion practised there
That all residents of Singapore are of Indian origin

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT given in the chapter as a sign of Indian influence in Thailand?
questions.a: A script based on Brahmi was adopted in the Malay Peninsula, in the 4th century CE, not in Thailand. The Chakri kings, Dvaravati and Suvarnabhumi Airport are Thai examples.
o: A script based on Brahmi adopted in the 4th century CE
The name of the Dvaravati culture

questions.q:
Match the name in Column A with its meaning or source in Column B.
Column A: 1. Dvaravati  2. Ayutthaya  3. Suvarnabhumi  4. Singapuram
Column B: a. The lion city  b. Named after Ayodhya  c. The golden land  d. Named after Dwarka
questions.a: Dvaravati comes from Dwarka, Ayutthaya from Ayodhya, Suvarnabhumi means the golden land and Singapuram means the lion city. Distractors swap the two city-based names or the golden land with the lion city.

questions.q: 'India spread her traditions peacefully.' Justify this with examples from at least three Southeast Asian countries.
questions.a: Thailand: place names such as Dvaravati and Ayutthaya, Chakri kings named Rama, Theravada Buddhism, Hindu stories in royal ceremonies. Malaysia: Brahmi-based script, Indian workers on plantations, 9 per cent Indian origin. Singapore: Tamil as an official language, Little India, 9 per cent Indian origin. Indonesia: Borobudur, the rupiah with Garuda, Nalanda and Muara Jambi link. In none of these does the chapter describe conquest; it describes trade, pilgrimage and culture.
s: Thailand example
Malaysia example
Singapore or Indonesia example
Names the means: trade, pilgrimage, culture
Concluding judgement

questions.q:
A geography club in Nagapattinam studies the earthquake under the Indian Ocean near Indonesia in December 2004 and the tsunami that followed. Its members want to use their first month to fill a gap that still exists in their town, and not to repeat what the region has already built.
(a) Which three Indian regions were hit hardest, according to the chapter?
(b) Using the chapter's figures, at most what share of the region's deaths were in India?
(c) Where is the centre that now alerts India and her neighbours, and what links does the network use?
(d) The club can either rehearse evacuation drills in the school or campaign for a new network of sensors and satellites. Which should it do first? Justify using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. (b) About 15,000 of more than 200,000, so at most 15,000 / 200,000 = 7.5 per cent. (c) The Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre in Hyderabad; a network of sensors, satellites and communication links. (d) Evacuation drills: the chapter says India and her neighbours have already set up the network and the Hyderabad centre alerts them, so the gap that remains is knowing how to act on an alert.
s: Part (a): Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Andaman and Nicobar
Part (b): 7.5 per cent at most
Part (c): Hyderabad, with sensors, satellites and communication links
Part (d): drills, because the network already exists

questions.q: Describe the Borobudur Stupa in Indonesia in three points drawn from the chapter.
questions.a: Built in stone in the 8th and 9th centuries CE; pyramidal shape in five enormous platforms with over 500 statues of the Buddha and smaller stupas; designed like a mandala; it is the world's largest Buddhist monument.
s: Period and material
Platforms and statues
Mandala design and world's largest Buddhist monument

questions.q:
The exchange committee of a Hyderabad school can pair with one school abroad. Singapore offers a city with parks and walkways where littering is fined, and heavy investment in India. Malaysia offers collaborations with India in palm oil, energy and IT. The committee wants the partner where its students are likely to meet more people of Indian origin. Suppose the host ward in Singapore has 1,20,000 residents and the host town in Malaysia has 2,50,000, and both match the chapter's share of Indian-origin residents.
(a) How many people of Indian origin live in the Singapore ward?
(b) How many live in the Malaysian town?
(c) Which area of Singapore houses many of them, and how did the Indian community in Malaysia come to settle there?
(d) Which country should the committee choose, given its aim? Support your answer with your numbers and one chapter fact.
questions.a: (a) 9 per cent of 1,20,000 = 10,800. (b) 9 per cent of 2,50,000 = 22,500. (c) Little India; in the 19th and 20th centuries many workers, mainly from south India, migrated to Malaysia to work on rubber plantations. (d) Malaysia: 22,500 is more than twice 10,800, and the Malaysian Indian community is prominent today, so students would meet more people of Indian origin.
s: Part (c): Little India; plantation workers from south India
Part (d): Malaysia, backed by 22,500 against 10,800 and a chapter fact

questions.q: Meera says, 'Indian influence in Southeast Asia can still be seen even in Malaysia, where Islam became the predominant religion by the 15th century.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says Hindu and Buddhist influences began early in Malaysia, with names such as the Srivijaya Kingdom and a script based on India's Brahmi script adopted around the 4th century CE. These influences remain visible in art and literature even though Islam became the predominant religion by the 15th century. The Indian community is also prominent today.
s: Verdict: agrees with Meera
Early influence: Srivijaya name or Brahmi-based script
Influence still visible in art and literature, and Islam predominant by the 15th century

questions.q: Compare Thailand and Malaysia on the following: their ancient link with India, the religion practised today, the Indian community and economic ties.
questions.a: Thailand: link since the 3rd century BCE through traders and scholars; Dvaravati and Ayutthaya names; Theravada Buddhism widely practised; the Trilateral Highway through Manipur and Myanmar. Malaysia: links for over two millennia; Srivijaya and a Brahmi-based script in the 4th century CE; Islam predominant by the 15th century; 9 per cent of the population of Indian origin, workers on rubber plantations; India one of its largest trading partners in palm oil, energy, infrastructure and IT.
s: Ancient link of both
Religion today in both
Indian community in Malaysia
Economic or connectivity ties of both
A comparison drawn

questions.q: Write one clue each for Thailand, Malaysia and Singapore so that a classmate can guess the country. Each clue must use a different Indian link from the chapter.
questions.a: Any correct clues, e.g. Thailand: kings are all named Rama; Malaysia: Indian workers on rubber plantations and a Brahmi-based script; Singapore: named after Singapuram, the lion city, with Little India.
s: Thailand clue correct
Malaysia clue correct
Singapore clue correct and each uses a different link

questions.q: What is an archipelago? Use Indonesia to explain.
questions.a: An extensive group of islands. Indonesia is not a single landmass: it has several large islands and over 17,000 smaller ones.
s: Defines archipelago as a group of islands
Uses Indonesia with several large and over 17,000 smaller islands

questions.q: (a) The name 'Singapore' comes from which ancient name, and what does it mean? (b) In what order did Singapore pass from British rule to being a separate nation, and in which year did it become one?
questions.a: (a) Singapuram, meaning 'lion city'. (b) It was a British colony, then a part of Malaysia, and eventually a separate nation in 1965.
s: Part (a): Singapuram, the lion city
Part (b): British colony, then part of Malaysia, then separate nation in 1965

questions.q: Why did India join Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Thailand and others to set up a network of sensors and satellites, and where is India's warning centre?
questions.a: The 2004 tsunami exposed the urgent need for better early warning systems. The Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre is in Hyderabad and alerts neighbouring countries too.
s: Reason: the 2004 tsunami showed the need for early warning
Hyderabad and alerts to neighbours

questions.q: (a) In which century did the Malay region adopt a script based on India's Brahmi script, and which religion became predominant by the 15th century? (b) Why did many Indian workers go to Malaysia in the 19th and 20th centuries?
questions.a: (a) The 4th century CE; Islam. (b) To work as labour on the rubber plantations; they were mainly from south India.
s: Part (a): 4th century CE and Islam
Part (b): labour on rubber plantations, mainly from south India

questions.q: (a) What does 'Suvarnabhumi' mean, and which islands and peninsula were known by this name? (b) Why did Indian traders go there?
questions.a: (a) The golden land; Java, Sumatra and Malaya. (b) In search of gold and other valuable resources.
s: Part (a): golden land; Java, Sumatra and Malaya
Part (b): gold and other valuable resources

questions.q: Anil, an exporter in Mumbai, wants to send goods to Afghanistan and Central Asia without depending on the direct land route. Which port, being developed with India's help, would give him better access?
questions.a: Chabahar Port in Iran gives India better access to Afghanistan and Central Asia. Quanzhou is a Chinese trading port, Muscat is in Oman and Yangon is in Myanmar.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Over 10 per cent of the population of Oman is of Indian origin.
2. Harappan traders carried copper from India to Oman.
3. Iran's ports were within easy reach of India's west coast.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are stated in the chapter. 2 is reversed: Oman is rich in copper and Harappan traders are thought to have brought it back to India.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Parsis of India have been a living link with ancient Persian culture.
Reason (R): The Avesta, the ancient sacred text of Zoroastrianism, has parallels with India's Rigveda.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the parallels between two texts do not explain why the Parsis of India are a living link.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: What does the Motishwar Mandir in Muscat tell us?
questions.a: It is a Shiva temple that the Hindu community was allowed to build in the early 20th century, reflecting the Indian community in Oman. It is not Buddhist, Harappan or Persian.
o: Hindus in Oman were allowed to build a Shiva temple in the early 20th century
A Buddhist stupa was built there by Harappan traders
A Persian fire temple was shared by Indians and Omanis
A Vishnu temple was set up by Mughal rulers

questions.q: A teacher says that one community in India is a living link with ancient Persian culture. Which community is she talking about?
questions.a: The chapter says the Parsis of India have been a living link with ancient Persian culture. Merchant communities from north-western India settled in Oman, not Iran.
o: Merchant communities from north-western India who settled in Oman
Tamil families who moved from Sri Lanka to Tamil Nadu
Bhutanese pilgrims who visit Bodh Gaya

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT named in the chapter as a cultural link between India and Iran?
questions.a: The chapter names the Avesta's parallels with the Rigveda, Persian as a court language of the Mughals and the Parsis as a living link. The Boduberu dance is a link with the Maldives, not Iran.
o: The Boduberu dance echoing Tamil folk rhythms
Persian used as a court language
Parallels between the Avesta and the Rigveda

questions.q: Differentiate between 'Parasika' and 'Parsis' as used in the chapter.
questions.a: Parasika is the name by which the Mahabharata mentions the Persians, while the Parsis are the community of India who are a living link with ancient Persian culture.
s: Parasika: Persians as named in the Mahabharata
Parsis: Indian community, a living link with Persian culture

questions.q: (a) Which port in Iran is India helping to develop? (b) Which two regions does it give India better access to, and which 1947 event had complicated India's direct land access to one of them?
questions.a: (a) Chabahar Port. (b) Afghanistan and Central Asia; the creation of Pakistan in 1947 complicated direct access to Afghanistan.
s: Part (a): Chabahar Port
Part (b): Afghanistan and Central Asia, and the creation of Pakistan in 1947

questions.q: State two ways in which India and Oman cooperate in defence.
questions.a: Oman is India's closest defence partner in the Gulf, the first in the region where India holds joint military exercises with all three armed forces; the two work together on Indian Ocean maritime security.
s: First way of defence cooperation
Second way, different from the first

questions.q: By what name does the Mahabharata mention the Persians, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The Mahabharata mentions Persians as Parasika. Gandhara and Kapisha are places in Afghanistan, and Suvarnabhumi is the golden land of Southeast Asia.

questions.q: What is thought to have been brought back to the Indus-Sarasvati cities by Harappan traders who visited Oman?
questions.a: Oman is rich in copper, so Harappan traders are thought to have brought back copper ingots for the coppersmiths. Gold was the draw in Southeast Asia, and spices and textiles are linked to Thailand.

questions.q: Riya says, 'India's contact with Oman is recent, because the Motishwar Mandir was allowed only in the early 20th century.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. The temple shows the permission given in the early 20th century, but the chapter traces contact between India and Oman back over 5,000 years to the Harappan civilisation, and copper ingots dated to the 3rd millennium BCE support it.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Contact over 5,000 years, from the Harappan civilisation
Copper ingot evidence or the temple correctly placed as a later event

questions.q:
Suppose Oman has a population of 50 lakh. The social science club in a Surat school is planning a talk on Oman with the theme 'the Oman link in the 3rd millennium BCE, the time of the copper ingot'. It can invite either a historian of the Harappan trade or an officer of the Navy.
(a) Using the chapter's share of Indian-origin people in Oman, at least how many Indian-origin people live there on the supposition?
(b) What material does the ingot consist of, and what does this suggest about Harappan trade?
(c) Name the Muscat temple and the century in which permission was given.
(d) Which speaker fits the club's theme? Justify using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Over 10 per cent of 50 lakh = more than 5 lakh. (b) Copper; Harappan traders are thought to have brought it back from Oman for the coppersmiths of the Indus-Sarasvati cities. (c) The Motishwar Mandir; the early 20th century. (d) The historian: the theme is the 3rd millennium BCE link of Harappan traders and copper, while the Navy officer's subject, joint exercises and maritime security with Oman as India's closest defence partner in the Gulf, belongs to the present.
s: Part (a): more than 5 lakh
Part (b): copper, brought by Harappan traders
Part (c): Motishwar Mandir, early 20th century
Part (d): the historian, because the theme is the Harappan period and the defence link is modern

questions.q: The closing note of the chapter names four ancient routes. Name them and say which regions they connected India with.
questions.a: The Uttarapatha, Dakshinapatha, the Silk Route and the spice routes. They connected India with Central Asia, Southeast Asia and the Arabian Peninsula, resulting in trade and cultural exchanges.
s: Names the four routes
Regions connected
Result: trade and cultural exchange

questions.q: India and Iran are called 'ancient neighbours'. Justify this with at least four pieces of evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: Ties since the Bronze Age through land routes via Pakistan and Afghanistan, which became part of the Silk Route; sea routes from Iran's ports to India's west coast; the Avesta's parallels with the Rigveda; the Mahabharata mentions Persians as Parasika; Persian used as a court language by the Mughals; the Parsis as a living link; modern cooperation in trade, energy, transport and Chabahar.
s: Bronze Age ties and the routes
Language and texts: Avesta, Rigveda, Persian
Parasika and the Parsis
Modern cooperation including Chabahar
A concluding judgement on why they are 'ancient'

questions.q: Write three clues that point to the answer 'Oman'. Each clue must use a different fact from the chapter.
questions.a: Any three: the Land of Copper; contact over 5,000 years since the Harappan civilisation; over 10 per cent of the people are of Indian origin; the Motishwar Mandir in Muscat; India's closest defence partner in the Gulf.
s: Clue 1 correct
Clue 2 correct and different
Clue 3 correct and the clues fit only Oman

questions.q:
A Mumbai firm has to deliver 600 tonnes of medical supplies to Kabul. Route A is the old direct land way through the country that lies between India and Afghanistan; it costs Rs 5,200 per tonne when open. Route B is by sea from India's west coast to a port in Iran that India is helping to develop, then by road; it costs Rs 3,400 per tonne by sea and Rs 1,500 per tonne by road. The firm wants the cheaper route that also gives dependable access.
(a) Which Iranian port would Route B use?
(b) What event in 1947 complicated direct land access between India and Afghanistan?
(c) Find the total cost of each route and the saving.
(d) Which route should the firm prefer? Support your answer with your figures and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Chabahar Port. (b) The creation of Pakistan in 1947. (c) Route A: 600 x 5,200 = Rs 31.2 lakh. Route B: 600 x (3,400 + 1,500) = 600 x 4,900 = Rs 29.4 lakh. Saving Rs 1.8 lakh. (d) Route B: it is cheaper by Rs 1.8 lakh, Iran's ports are within easy reach of India's west coast, and the chapter says Chabahar gives India better access to Afghanistan, whereas direct access has been complicated since 1947.
s: Part (a): Chabahar
Part (b): the creation of Pakistan
Part (c): Rs 31.2 lakh, Rs 29.4 lakh and a saving of Rs 1.8 lakh
Part (d): Route B, on cost and on the access the chapter describes

questions.q: Compare India's links with Iran and with Oman on four points: the age of contact, the route or trade involved, the cultural or community link, and present-day cooperation.
questions.a: Iran: Bronze Age ties; land routes becoming the Silk Route and sea routes; Avesta, Persian, Parsis; trade, energy, transport and Chabahar. Oman: over 5,000 years, the Harappan civilisation; copper ingots brought back by sea; over 10 per cent of the population of Indian origin and the Motishwar Mandir; the closest defence partner in the Gulf and maritime security work.
s: Age of contact for both
Route or trade for both
Cultural or community links for both
Present-day cooperation for both
Comparison or conclusion

questions.q: How old is the contact between India and Oman, which civilisation marks its start, and why did its traders visit Oman?
questions.a: People-to-people contact goes back over 5,000 years to the Indus or Harappan civilisation; Oman is rich in copper, so traders are thought to have gone for copper ingots.
s: Over 5,000 years, Harappan civilisation
Oman rich in copper; traders brought copper ingots

questions.q: (a) Through which present-day countries did the early land routes between India and Iran pass, and what did these routes become part of? (b) Why were sea routes also easy to use?
questions.a: (a) Pakistan and Afghanistan; the Silk Route. (b) Iran's ports were within easy reach of India's west coast.
s: Part (a): Pakistan and Afghanistan; the Silk Route
Part (b): Iran's ports close to India's west coast
